paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning algorithms add regularization to the problem of choosing actions. Entropy and Kullback–Leibler divergence are common choices, but studying each algorithm separately can obscure their shared structure. This paper develops a general theory of regularized Markov decision processes that brings a wider range of these choices into one framework.

The theory also covers modified policy iteration, an approach broad enough to include both policy iteration and value iteration. Its central tools are a regularized Bellman operator and the Legendre–Fenchel transform from convex optimization. Together, these provide a way to describe regularized updates and analyze how errors propagate through repeated learning steps.

The framework encompasses general algorithmic schemes that include, sometimes through variants, Trust Region Policy Optimization, Soft Q-learning, Stochastic Actor Critic, and Dynamic Policy Programming. It also connects these reinforcement learning methods with proximal optimization, particularly Mirror Descent. The contribution is a common analytical foundation for understanding related algorithms and their error behavior.
icml-2019-a-theory-of-regularized-markov.tldr: A general theory connects regularized reinforcement learning algorithms and enables analysis of how their errors propagate.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes provide a way to select sets that balance individual item quality with diversity across the selected items. This is useful in recommendation and information retrieval, but repeatedly drawing such sets can be expensive. Standard sampling takes time proportional to the collection size after preprocessing, and personalization can invalidate that preparatory work.

The paper introduces a tree-based sampling method that changes this trade-off. It spends slightly more effort on preprocessing so that subsequent samples take time logarithmic in the number of items. An extension supports arbitrary feature weights supplied at query time, allowing the same approach to produce personalized samples while retaining that logarithmic dependence.

In experiments with collections of 100,000 items and samples containing 10 items, the method runs more than 300 times faster than traditional DPP sampling. That result illustrates the practical benefit of preparing for repeated sampling in advance. The contribution also addresses personalization directly, so its speed advantage is not restricted to repeatedly serving an unchanged selection preference.
icml-2019-a-tree-based-method-for-fast-r.tldr: A tree-based DPP sampler supports fast repeated and personalized sampling with logarithmic dependence on collection size after preprocessing.

paragraphs: A classifier can fail when an input is deliberately modified to fool it, even if the original input was classified correctly. It can also fail when an image receives random corruption, such as additive Gaussian noise. This paper investigates whether these apparently different weaknesses reflect a shared underlying phenomenon.

The authors provide both theoretical and empirical evidence connecting adversarial examples with errors on noisy inputs. Their analysis brings adversarial robustness and corruption robustness into a common discussion: the model's behavior under random disturbance is relevant to understanding its vulnerability to deliberately chosen disturbance. The claimed connection concerns these forms of failure, rather than merely their similar appearance.

This perspective suggests that progress against adversarial examples should accompany better performance under broader, realistic image corruptions. It also motivates test error on noisy image distributions as a computationally manageable metric for evaluating defenses. The proposed metric gives researchers another way to examine robustness, while the evidence supports a relationship between the two research directions rather than an unconditional promise about every defense.
icml-2019-adversarial-examples-are-a-nat.tldr: Theoretical and empirical evidence links adversarial vulnerability to errors under random noise, motivating noisy test error as a defense evaluation metric.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often approximates a posterior distribution and then uses that approximation to estimate an expectation. When the function being averaged is already known, this pipeline can spend effort approximating aspects of the posterior that are less useful for the final calculation. AMCI instead amortizes the integration task directly.

The method learns three separate proposal distributions, each adapted to a different component of the expectation calculation. At runtime, it draws samples from each proposal and combines them into one estimate. This makes the eventual quantity of interest part of how the sampling machinery is prepared, rather than treating posterior approximation as the sole objective.

The authors show that AMCI can theoretically achieve arbitrarily small errors for any integrable target function with one runtime sample from each proposal. This is a possibility result, not a guarantee for every learned proposal. On several example problems, it empirically outperforms even the theoretically optimal self-normalized importance sampler. The framework can amortize across both datasets and target functions.
icml-2019-amortized-monte-carlo-integrat.tldr: AMCI learns three proposals tailored to expectation estimation, enabling more accurate integration than posterior-focused approaches in the reported examples.

paragraphs: Topic modeling seeks to recover an underlying organization of data into topics. Naive mean field variational inference is a widely used way to approximate the associated uncertainty. This paper shows that, in certain ranges of model parameters, the approximation can produce an apparently meaningful topic decomposition even when the data contain no information about the true decomposition.

In those regimes, the algorithm's output is uncorrelated with the actual topics. The issue therefore reaches beyond finding an imperfect version of an identifiable pattern: the method can present structure where the available data do not support recovering that structure. A nontrivial output alone is not evidence that the true topics have been learned.

The instability also affects uncertainty estimates. The estimated posterior mean is incorrect, and credible regions fail to attain their nominal coverage. The authors discuss how more accurate mean field approximations remedy the instability. These findings identify a specific failure mode of the naive approximation, with consequences for both the reported topic structure and the confidence attached to it.
icml-2019-an-instability-in-variational-.tldr: In certain parameter regimes, naive mean field inference reports unsupported topic structure and miscalibrated uncertainty.

paragraphs: This paper examines neural network training through the Hessian, which describes how the training objective curves around the current parameters. Rather than considering only a single curvature value, the authors track the distribution of Hessian eigenvalues throughout optimization. This view reveals how different directions in parameter space behave as training proceeds.

For networks without batch normalization, the authors observe large, isolated eigenvalues appearing rapidly. They also find that much of the gradient lies in the corresponding eigenspaces, linking the directions emphasized by training to these unusually strong curvature directions. In a batch-normalized network, both effects are almost absent. A theoretical rationale explains part of this observed contrast.

To make this investigation feasible at scale, the authors adapt numerical linear algebra techniques for accurately estimating the entire Hessian spectrum of ImageNet-scale networks. The resulting contribution combines an empirical account of optimization geometry with a scalable measurement method. The observations illuminate differences associated with batch normalization, while the proposed theory is explicitly a partial explanation.
icml-2019-an-investigation-into-neural-n.tldr: Scalable Hessian-spectrum estimates reveal strong curvature and gradient concentration effects that are almost absent with batch normalization.

paragraphs: Training examples can contribute differently to a predictor's performance, raising the question of how to assign value to individual data points. This paper introduces data Shapley as a principled valuation measure for supervised learning. Its values concern a datum's contribution to the performance of a predictor produced by a given learning algorithm.

The authors show that the measure uniquely satisfies several natural properties of equitable data valuation. To make it useful with large datasets and complex learners, including neural networks, they develop Monte Carlo and gradient-based estimation methods. These methods connect the valuation framework to settings where computing individual contributions directly would be computationally demanding.

Experiments on biomedical, image, and synthetic data show stronger insight into task-specific data value than leave-one-out valuation or leverage scores. Low-valued examples help identify outliers and corrupted data, while high-valued examples indicate what kinds of additional data could improve the predictor. These results make valuation useful for data inspection and acquisition as well as for reasoning about equitable contributions.
icml-2019-data-shapley-equitable-valuati.tldr: Data Shapley assigns principled values to training examples and helps identify problematic data and promising acquisition targets.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often receive observations with many dimensions even when the underlying situation admits a much smaller description. DeepMDP formalizes learning such a continuous latent state space. The aim is to produce a compact representation that supports reasoning about the environment through its rewards and future behavior.

A DeepMDP is trained using two tractable losses: one for predicting rewards and another for predicting the distribution of the next latent state. These objectives tie representation learning to quantities that matter for interaction. The authors establish theoretical guarantees connecting their optimization to both the quality of the state embedding and the quality of the learned environment model.

The experiments examine these ideas in two ways. In a synthetic environment, a trained DeepMDP recovers the latent structure behind high-dimensional observations. In Atari 2600 tasks, learning a DeepMDP as an auxiliary objective produces large improvements over model-free reinforcement learning. Together, these findings support using reward and latent-transition prediction to learn useful representations.
icml-2019-deepmdp-learning-continuous-la.tldr: DeepMDP learns compact state representations through reward and latent-transition prediction, with theoretical guarantees and reported reinforcement learning gains.

paragraphs: Dropout is commonly used to reduce overfitting when training large neural networks. This paper studies its effects by separating two parts of training that are usually considered together: the forward pass that computes the network's output and the backward pass that supplies the information used to update its parameters.

The authors find that these two passes need different levels of noise to improve generalization. That observation changes the design question from how much dropout to use overall to how dropout should act at each stage. It suggests that understanding dropout's benefit requires examining both prediction computation and the backward training signal, rather than treating their perturbations as one undifferentiated effect.

Based on this finding, the paper proposes augmented dropout, which uses different dropping strategies in the forward and backward passes. Experiments verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and practical: separating the two passes reveals a useful distinction, and that distinction motivates a modified training technique.
icml-2019-demystifying-dropout-667fa61fb.tldr: Augmented dropout uses different dropping strategies in the forward and backward passes, motivated by their differing noise needs.

paragraphs: A feature can be associated with an outcome across an entire dataset yet cease to be relevant within a particular subgroup. This paper studies conditional feature selection, where relevance depends on the values of other features. The goal is to identify these local differences instead of reporting only one globally relevant feature set.

The authors extend the knockoff procedure to select features conditionally while controlling an appropriate generalization of the false discovery rate. This provides statistical protection against false selections in the conditional setting. By using the knockoff framework without specifying a feature-to-response model, the method preserves the quality of the stated guarantee when moving from global to conditional selection.

The implementation includes an algorithm that automatically partitions feature space to make differences between selected feature sets more pronounced across regions. Experiments validate the theoretical statistical results. The contribution combines a more detailed account of feature relevance with error control, so discovering different associations in different contexts need not mean abandoning the framework's statistical guarantees.
icml-2019-discovering-conditionally-sali.tldr: An extended knockoff method discovers context-dependent feature relevance while controlling a conditional false discovery rate.

paragraphs: Gradient descent often works well on nonconvex learning problems, even though general theory cannot exclude convergence to poor critical points. This paper investigates why it can succeed in the structured setting of complete orthogonal dictionary learning. The authors analyze the geometry of the objective to connect the optimization landscape with algorithmic behavior.

They prove that randomly initialized gradient descent converges to a neighborhood of a global optimum. The convergence rates grow as low-order polynomials in dimension, despite the objective having exponentially many saddle points. The result shows that a large number of saddles does not, by itself, force inefficient optimization in this particular problem.

The explanation centers on negative curvature in directions normal to the stable manifolds associated with saddle points. This geometric feature helps account for efficient convergence despite the saddles. The paper also provides evidence that other important nonconvex problems share this feature. That broader evidence suggests a useful perspective, while the stated convergence guarantee concerns complete orthogonal dictionary learning.
icml-2019-efficient-dictionary-learning-.tldr: For complete orthogonal dictionary learning, randomly initialized gradient descent efficiently approaches a global optimum despite exponentially many saddles.

paragraphs: Large language models can benefit from abundant data for unsupervised pre-training, but training their many parameters remains costly even on powerful hardware. This paper explores a faster way to train BERT by progressively increasing model depth. Its starting point is an examination of how attention behaves inside an already trained model.

The authors visualize attention distributions across layers and positions. They find that, in most layers, attention concentrates near the current position and around the start-of-sentence token. Motivated by this observed pattern, they introduce a stacking algorithm that transfers knowledge from a shallow model into a deeper one, then apply that procedure progressively during training.

Experiments show that this training strategy produces models with performance similar to models trained from scratch while requiring much less training time. The practical idea is to use a learned shallow model as the basis for deeper training. The reported result supports progressive stacking as an effective way to improve BERT training efficiency without a substantial change in the observed performance.
icml-2019-efficient-training-of-bert-by-.tldr: Progressively transferring a shallow BERT model into deeper models substantially speeds training while achieving similar reported performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate mutual information between a neural network's input and a hidden representation. It first considers feedforward networks with fixed weights and noisy internal representations, developing a rigorous estimation framework. The analysis relates this information measurement to transmission through an additive white Gaussian noise channel.

Within that framework, the authors connect decreasing mutual information during training to geometric clustering: representations of examples from the same class progressively gather together. Experiments verify this connection. This gives the measured compression a concrete geometric interpretation, relating an abstract information quantity to how samples are arranged in representation space.

The paper then examines deterministic networks, where the mutual information quantity is provably uninformative for this purpose. These networks still form same-class clusters, and the binning approximation used in earlier compression studies is identified as a clustering measure. The authors consequently provide new evidence that compression and generalization may not be causally related. This challenges a causal interpretation without claiming to establish that no such relationship can ever exist.
icml-2019-estimating-information-flow-in.tldr: The paper connects measured information compression to representation clustering and questions whether compression causally explains generalization.

paragraphs: Scattering transforms extract features from signals such as images and audio. This paper explores extending that approach to graph data, paralleling the move from conventional convolutional networks to geometric deep learning. The central question is whether the resulting graph features preserve useful information for analyzing individual graphs and collections of graphs.

The authors focus on retaining informative variation and relationships in the data. A useful representation must preserve distinctions that matter for analysis, including relationships between separate graphs and patterns visible in aggregate. They also relate their construction to earlier theoretical results establishing stability of similar transforms under families of graph deformations, connecting feature usefulness with robustness to structural changes.

The paper demonstrates geometric scattering features in two settings: classification of social network graphs and exploratory analysis of biochemical data. These applications illustrate both predictive and exploratory uses of the representation. The stated contribution is an extension of scattering to graphs and an examination of the information those features retain, supported by application demonstrations and connections to existing stability theory.
icml-2019-geometric-scattering-for-graph.tldr: Geometric scattering extends signal feature extraction to graphs for classification and exploration while examining retained information and stability connections.

paragraphs: One way to find structure in a large network is to identify regions with many edges. This paper targets two fundamental problems used in that approach: finding a densest subgraph and computing a k-core decomposition. Both support density-based analysis, but processing very large networks makes algorithmic scalability a central concern.

The authors design algorithms for the massively parallel computation model. Their improvements concern how efficiently these network problems can be solved across parallel computation rounds. For k-core decomposition, they report an exponential improvement over the referenced prior algorithm. For densest subgraph, their result uses quadratically fewer rounds than the cited earlier work.

These are improvements relative to specific previous methods within the stated computation model, rather than a universal claim about every network clustering procedure. The authors complement the algorithmic analysis with experiments examining scalability. Together, the results address the computational machinery behind density-based network analysis: faster parallel solutions to these foundational problems can make the corresponding structural analysis more practical at large scales.
icml-2019-improved-parallel-algorithms-f.tldr: New massively parallel algorithms improve the round complexity of densest subgraph and k-core decomposition over the cited prior methods.

paragraphs: A large dataset may contain more examples than are needed to characterize a model's optimal parameters. This paper investigates that form of compressibility: how much of a dataset can be represented by a smaller collection of informative samples. The question matters for machine learning and for optimization distributed across a network.

The proposed framework learns two things jointly: the mapping from inputs to outputs and the samples that most effectively represent the dataset. The authors call this selected collection a sufficient dataset. Their analysis shows that its size grows sublinearly with the size of the original dataset, meaning the required collection grows more slowly than the full data under their analytical result.

Numerical evaluations on real datasets report compression of up to 95% without a noticeable deterioration in generalization error. That figure describes the reported evaluations rather than a guaranteed reduction for every dataset. The findings support treating sample selection as part of learning itself, with the possibility of retaining predictive performance using substantially fewer examples.
icml-2019-learning-and-data-selection-in.tldr: Jointly learning a predictor and representative samples yields sublinear sufficient-dataset growth and substantial compression in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Turning a musical score or rhythm into an expressive performance requires recovering details that an abstract description leaves out. This paper explores that translation using sequence-to-sequence models and recurrent variational information bottleneck models. A central challenge is obtaining aligned training pairs that connect simplified musical inputs with expressive outputs.

The authors create paired data by applying simple transformations to performances, then train generative models to plausibly reverse those transformations. In drumming, operations such as quantizing timing or removing voices have clear musical meanings. The original performance supplies the paired target, making the transformation itself a way to generate training examples for the inverse task.

To support this work, the authors release a dataset containing more than 13 hours of professional drum performances, aligned with detailed timing and dynamics information. They also explore creative applications and report improvements over state-of-the-art methods for humanization, the task of producing a performance from a score. The contribution links a practical paired-data construction method with expressive musical generation.
icml-2019-learning-to-groove-with-invers.tldr: Models learn expressive drumming by reversing simple musical transformations, supported by a new professional-performance dataset.

paragraphs: Phase synchronization estimates a collection of alignment angles from noisy comparisons between pairs. Because the comparisons are noisy, the challenge is to obtain a jointly consistent set of estimates. This paper formulates the task as a nonconvex optimization problem that enforces consistency across multiple frequency channels.

The authors develop a two-stage algorithm inspired by harmonic retrieval in signal processing. Its distinguishing feature is the use of information from several frequency channels within the same synchronization procedure. The extra channels supply information that the algorithm can combine, while the formulation explicitly requires the pairwise comparisons to remain consistent across those channels.

The paper reports both theoretical and practical evidence of substantial improvement over state-of-the-art phase synchronization algorithms, with a mild additional computational cost from using the extra channels. The authors also extend the framework to synchronization over compact Lie groups, broadening its mathematical scope beyond alignment angles. The stated result is a favorable accuracy–computation trade-off for using richer frequency information in the synchronization problem.
icml-2019-multi-frequency-phase-synchron.tldr: A two-stage synchronization algorithm combines multiple frequency channels to improve alignment estimates with mild additional computation.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions as information arrives, before the full future is available. This paper studies how predictions from multiple experts, including machine learning algorithms, can improve those decisions. It focuses on the classical rent-or-buy problem, also known as ski rental, where an algorithm must choose between continuing to rent and committing to a purchase.

The authors develop algorithms that use the expert predictions and prove performance improvements over the adversarial scenario. This makes advice a formal part of the online decision problem: the analysis asks what improvement is achievable when predictions are available, rather than evaluating a forecasting system independently of the decisions it supports.

The paper also proves matching lower bounds. Within the studied setting, these establish that the algorithms attain the best possible performance described by the bounds. Experiments provide an empirical check of their practical behavior. The contribution therefore combines a way to use multiple experts with both achievable guarantees and limits on how much an algorithm can improve.
icml-2019-online-algorithms-for-rent-or-.tldr: Expert-assisted rent-or-buy algorithms achieve provable improvements over the adversarial setting, with matching lower bounds.

paragraphs: The step sizes available to JacSketch variance-reduced gradient methods depend on an expected smoothness constant. Knowing this quantity in advance can justify larger steps and faster convergence. This paper provides simple closed-form expressions and bounds for that quantity, then examines them through numerical experiments.

Because SAGA belongs to the JacSketch family, the authors use the bounds to recommend choices of both step size and mini-batch size. Their proposed practice is competitive with numerical grid search. The contribution turns an analytical quantity into practical parameter guidance, reducing the need to determine useful settings solely by trying many alternatives.

The analysis also shows that SAGA's total complexity decreases linearly as mini-batch size increases up to a specified optimal value. The improvement is explicitly limited to that range; it does not imply that ever-larger batches keep helping. The authors conjecture that similar behavior holds for many other stochastic variance-reduced methods, with their expected-smoothness analysis offering a possible route to proving it.
icml-2019-optimal-mini-batch-and-step-si.tldr: Expected-smoothness bounds guide SAGA tuning and establish linear complexity improvements up to an optimal mini-batch size.

paragraphs: Associations between measured variables can be distorted by other observed variables that act as confounders. This paper introduces a partially linear additive Gaussian graphical model, or PLA-GGM, to estimate associations in that setting. The goal is to learn a graphical description while accounting for the influence of the observed confounders.

A key feature is that the approach avoids imposing parametric constraints on how confounders affect the estimated graph structure. This gives the adjustment more flexibility than requiring those effects to follow a prescribed parametric form. The authors estimate the model using MaPPLE, an L1-regularized maximal pseudo-profile likelihood estimator, and prove a square-root-n sparsistency result for it.

The theoretical result concerns recovery of sparse structure, connecting the estimator to the graph-learning objective. The authors also evaluate PLA-GGM on synthetic and real-world datasets, reporting better performance than competing methods in those experiments. Together, the contributions combine flexible treatment of observed confounding with a statistically analyzed estimator and empirical evidence for improved association estimation.
icml-2019-partially-linear-additive-gaus.tldr: PLA-GGM estimates associations under observed confounding using flexible confounder effects and a sparsistency-backed regularized estimator.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can be difficult to deploy when memory or communication is limited. This paper studies how much a trained model can be compressed while controlling the resulting loss in performance. It uses rate-distortion theory to give compression a principled foundation and improve objectives used by methods such as pruning and quantization.

The authors prove a lower bound on the rate-distortion function for model compression and show that the bound is achievable for linear models. The achieving construction is computationally intractable in practice. Its role is nevertheless useful: the analysis motivates a new compression objective that can guide practical compressors.

The paper also proves optimality of the proposed scheme for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks. Experiments show an improved compression–accuracy trade-off relative to the baseline. These contributions connect a theoretical limit with a usable design principle, while keeping distinct the intractable construction, the stated optimality result for a particular network class, and the empirical improvement obtained in practice.
icml-2019-rate-distortion-for-model-comp.tldr: Rate-distortion analysis motivates a practical compression objective with theoretical optimality results and an improved empirical compression–accuracy trade-off.

paragraphs: A complex modular network can process inputs through many interacting components. This paper proposes compact summaries, called sketches, that retain essential information about that processing and the network's inputs and outputs. The sketches support quick identification of important components and input summary statistics without requiring the full description to be inspected at once.

Their recursive structure allows a component's sketch to be unpacked into subcomponents, capturing potentially complicated directed acyclic graph relationships. They also retain high-weight information when a fraction of the sketch is erased at random. This graceful degradation makes the summary useful even when only part of its original content remains.

Collections of sketches can serve as an implicit knowledge graph, supporting retrieval of related sketches and discovery of emerging concepts through new clusters in sketch space. Finally, for the task of learning a ground-truth deep network, the authors show that adding sketches to input–output examples can theoretically make learning easier. The proposal thus connects compact representation, structured retrieval, and learning support.
icml-2019-recursive-sketches-for-modular.tldr: Recursive sketches compactly summarize modular network processing, support related-content retrieval, and can theoretically aid learning a ground-truth network.

paragraphs: Selective prediction allows a model to decline some predictions instead of answering on every input. The central trade-off is between coverage, the portion of inputs it accepts, and risk on those accepted inputs. This paper introduces SelectiveNet, a deep network architecture that makes rejection part of the learning process itself.

Many existing rejection methods place a confidence threshold on a network that has already been trained. SelectiveNet jointly learns the prediction task and the rejection decision through end-to-end training. It supports classification or regression, and the resulting network is optimized for the covered domain: the inputs on which it chooses to provide an answer.

Experiments across several classification and regression datasets show consistently better risk–coverage trade-offs, including new state-of-the-art results for deep selective classification. The significance is that deciding where to answer can influence training, rather than being added only afterward. The reported findings support learning prediction and selection together when the objective is accuracy over a chosen portion of the input domain.
icml-2019-selectivenet-a-deep-neural-net.tldr: SelectiveNet jointly learns predictions and rejection, improving reported error–coverage trade-offs on classification and regression tasks.

paragraphs: Unlabeled data reveal how inputs are distributed without directly providing their desired outputs. This paper asks how much that knowledge can reduce the number of labeled examples needed for learning. It compares learning with and without exact knowledge of the input distribution, isolating the informational value of knowing where data come from.

For the class of projections on an n-dimensional Boolean hypercube, the authors prove a multiplicative separation of order log n in labeled sample requirements. For the class containing all functions on a domain of any size, they prove that there is no separation. These contrasting results show that the value of distribution knowledge depends on the class being learned.

Exact distribution knowledge is an idealized version of semi-supervised learning in which unlabeled data are sufficiently plentiful to reveal the distribution completely. The results therefore quantify the value of unlabeled information in that ideal setting. They establish that even this strong knowledge can help for one function class while providing no separation for another.
icml-2019-the-information-theoretic-valu.tldr: Exact input-distribution knowledge yields a logarithmic labeled-sample separation for Boolean projections but none for the class of all functions.
